Apple___Apple_scab.cause: Fungus: Venturia inaequalis. Spreads through rain splash and wind. Survives winter in fallen leaves.
Apple___Apple_scab.spread_rate: Can infect 60-80% of fruits in 2-3 weeks during wet weather (temperatures 10-24°C with rainfall)
Apple___Apple_scab.symptoms: Olive-green to brown velvety spots on leaves and fruits. Leaves may curl and drop early. Fruit develops dark, scabby, corky patches — unmarketable.
Apple___Apple_scab.treatment_organic:
**Spray schedule:**
- Sulfur dust 80 WP @ 3 grams per litre of water
- Spray 200 litres per acre
- Repeat every 7-10 days during wet season
- Bordeaux mixture 1% (copper sulfate + lime) as preventive

**Cultural:** Remove and burn fallen leaves in October. Do not compost infected material.
Apple___Apple_scab.treatment_chemical:
**Primary:** Mancozeb 75 WP @ **2.5 grams per litre** · spray 200 litres/acre · repeat every 10 days

**Systemic (curative):** Myclobutanil 10 WP @ **1 gram per litre** · penetrates leaf tissue · apply within 72 hours of rain

**Captan:** Captan 50 WP @ **2 grams per litre** · excellent for fruit protection

⚠️ **Do NOT spray** within 14 days of harvest
⚠️ **Rotate chemicals** — do not use Mancozeb more than 4 consecutive sprays
Apple___Apple_scab.dosage_summary: Mancozeb 75 WP: 2.5g/L water · 200L per acre · every 10 days
Apple___Apple_scab.cost_estimate: ₹300–450 per acre per spray · Full season (8 sprays): ₹2,400–3,600
Apple___Apple_scab.days_to_recovery: New leaves stop showing symptoms in 10-14 days. Existing fruit lesions do not heal — prevent new infection.
Apple___Apple_scab.prevention:
- Plant resistant varieties: Priam, Liberty, Redfree
- Prune trees for good air circulation
- Collect and burn all fallen leaves before winter
- Apply dormant copper spray before bud break in February
Apple___Apple_scab.source: ICAR-CISH · Maharashtra Horticulture Mission · Apple Scab Management Guidelines

Apple___Black_rot.cause: Fungus: Botryosphaeria obtusa. Enters through wounds, insect damage, hail. Cankers on wood survive year-round.
Apple___Black_rot.spread_rate: Infected fruit becomes completely rotten in 5-7 days. Spreads rapidly in warm (21-30°C) humid weather.
Apple___Black_rot.symptoms: Brown to purple sunken spots on fruit starting from calyx end. Fruit shrivels to black 'mummy'. Leaves show 'frog-eye' spots — purple borders with tan centres. Cankers on bark.
Apple___Black_rot.treatment_organic:
**No effective organic cure once infection starts.**

**Prevention:**
- Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3g/L as protective spray
- Remove all mummified fruits from tree and ground
- Prune out dead wood and cankers 15cm below infection
- Disinfect pruning tools with 10% bleach between cuts
Apple___Black_rot.treatment_chemical:
**Captan 50 WP @ 2g/L** · spray 200L/acre · protective spray before infection

**Thiophanate-methyl 70 WP @ 1.5g/L** · systemic curative · apply at petal fall and every 14 days

**Ziram 76 WG @ 3g/L** · for canker management on bark

⚠️ **Do NOT spray** within 7 days of harvest
Apple___Black_rot.dosage_summary: Captan 50 WP: 2g/L · 200L/acre · every 14 days during season
Apple___Black_rot.cost_estimate: ₹400–600 per acre per spray · Season cost: ₹3,200–4,800 (8 sprays)
Apple___Black_rot.days_to_recovery: New infections stop in 14-21 days with proper spray program. Infected fruit cannot be saved.
Apple___Black_rot.prevention:
- Remove mummified fruits before winter
- Prune all dead and cankered wood in December-January
- Maintain good tree vigor with proper nutrition
- Avoid mechanical wounds during hail storms
Apple___Black_rot.source: ICAR-CISH Lucknow · Fruit Disease Management Compendium

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.cause: Fungus: Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae. Requires both apple AND cedar/juniper trees to complete life cycle. Spores spread by wind.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.spread_rate: Lesions develop in 9-11 days after infection. Spreads over 2-3 km by wind from nearby cedar trees.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.symptoms: Bright orange-yellow spots on upper leaf surface in April-May. Small tube-like structures (aecia) on lower leaf. Fruit shows orange lesions near calyx.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.treatment_organic:
- Remove cedar/juniper trees within 500 metres if possible
- Sulfur 80 WP @ 3g/L from pink bud stage through June
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.treatment_chemical:
**Myclobutanil 10 WP @ 1g/L** — most effective, apply at pink bud, bloom, and every 7-10 days

**Propiconazole 25 EC @ 1ml/L** — systemic, apply from bud break

⚠️ Apply BEFORE orange spots appear — chemical cannot cure existing lesions
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.dosage_summary: Myclobutanil 10 WP: 1g/L · 200L/acre · from pink bud through June
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.cost_estimate: ₹500–700 per acre for full season program
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.days_to_recovery: Existing spots do not disappear. New leaves protected within 5-7 days of spray.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.prevention:
- Plant resistant varieties: Liberty, Enterprise, Redfree
- Remove infected twigs from nearby junipers in February-March

Apple___healthy.symptoms: Leaf appears healthy — deep green colour, no spots or lesions.
Apple___healthy.treatment_organic: No treatment required. Maintain good orchard hygiene.
Apple___healthy.prevention:
- Continue regular monitoring every 7 days
- Maintain balanced fertilization
- Ensure good drainage and air circulation

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.cause: Fungus: Podosphaera clandestina. Thrives in warm days (20-27°C) and cool nights. High humidity without rain favours spread.
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.spread_rate: Spreads in 5-7 days to cover entire shoot. Can infect 40-60% of canopy in 3 weeks if untreated.
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.symptoms: White powdery coating on young leaves, shoots, and fruit. Leaves curl and become distorted. Affected shoots stunted. Fruit develops russet skin patches.
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.treatment_organic:
- Sulfur 80 WP @ 3g/L · spray every 7-10 days · avoid applying in temperatures above 32°C
- Potassium bicarbonate 5g/L as alternative
- Neem oil 5ml/L at first sign
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.treatment_chemical:
**Hexaconazole 5 EC @ 1ml/L** — systemic, apply at first sign of disease

**Triadimefon 25 WP @ 1g/L** — effective curative at early stage

**Tebuconazole 25.9 EC @ 1ml/L** — best for fruit protection period

⚠️ **Do NOT spray sulfur** when temperature above 35°C — leaf burn
⚠️ **Do NOT spray** within 7 days of harvest
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.days_to_recovery: White coating stops spreading in 5-7 days. Existing lesions fade in 14-21 days.
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.prevention:
- Prune to improve air circulation in canopy
- Avoid excessive nitrogen — promotes susceptible soft growth
- Apply preventive sulfur spray before disease appears

Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.symptoms: Healthy green leaf with no lesions.

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.cause: Fungus: Cercospora zeae-maydis. Survives in crop residue. Spreads rapidly in humid conditions with temperatures 25-30°C.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.spread_rate: Can destroy 50-70% of leaf area in 3-4 weeks. Yield loss up to 40-60% in severe cases — one of the most damaging maize diseases.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.symptoms: Long, rectangular grey-brown lesions (5-70mm) running parallel to leaf veins. Lesions have defined edges. Entire leaf turns brown and dies from bottom up. Severe lodging risk.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.treatment_organic:
- Trichoderma viride seed treatment @ 4g/kg seed before sowing
- Crop rotation — do NOT grow maize in same field 2 consecutive years
- Deep ploughing to bury infected stubble
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.treatment_chemical:
**Azoxystrobin 23 SC @ 1ml/L** — most effective, apply at VT (tasseling) stage

**Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5g/L** — preventive, spray 200L/acre at 10-leaf stage and tasseling

**Propiconazole 25 EC @ 1ml/L** — curative for early infection

⚠️ **Critical spray timing** — apply at first sign of lower leaf infection. Spraying after 30% canopy affected gives poor results.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.dosage_summary: Azoxystrobin 23 SC: 1ml/L · 200L/acre · at tasseling and 14 days later
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.days_to_recovery: New leaves remain healthy in 10-14 days. Affected lower leaves do not recover — protect upper canopy.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.prevention:
- Plant resistant hybrids (DK 9133, Pioneer 30V92)
- Avoid dense sowing — maintain 60cm row spacing
- Remove and burn infected crop residue after harvest
- 2-year rotation with soybean or wheat
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.source: ICAR-IIMR Hyderabad · Maize Disease Management Bulletin

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.cause: Fungus: Puccinia sorghi. Spores spread rapidly by wind over long distances. Favoured by cool temperatures (15-25°C) and high humidity.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.spread_rate: Spreads across entire field in 7-10 days in favourable weather. Can reduce yield by 20-40% if infection occurs before tasseling.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.symptoms: Brick-red to brown oval pustules (2-4mm) scattered on both surfaces of leaves. Pustules rupture and release orange-red powdery spores. Severely infected leaves turn yellow and die.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.treatment_organic:
- Sulfur dust 80 WP @ 3g/L as protective spray
- Apply when pustules first appear on lower leaves
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.treatment_chemical:
**Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5g/L** — standard protective spray, 200L/acre

**Propiconazole 25 EC @ 1ml/L** — systemic curative, very effective

**Tebuconazole 25.9 EC @ 1ml/L** — best if infection already established

⚠️ Spray within 5 days of first pustule appearance for best results
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.dosage_summary: Propiconazole 25 EC: 1ml/L · 200L/acre · repeat after 14 days if needed
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.days_to_recovery: Rust stops spreading in 7-10 days. New pustules stop forming after 2nd spray.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.prevention:
- Plant resistant hybrids: HQPM-1, Vivek-23
- Early sowing (June 15-30) avoids peak rust season
- Avoid over-application of nitrogen — promotes susceptible tissue

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.cause: Fungus: Exserohilum turcicum. Survives in infected crop debris. Spreads by wind and rain splash in temperatures 18-27°C with high humidity.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.spread_rate: Lesions expand 2-3cm per day in favourable conditions. Can destroy 60-80% of leaf area in 2-3 weeks. Yield loss 20-50% when infection occurs before silking.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.symptoms: Large, cigar-shaped tan/grey lesions (10-15cm long) with wavy edges running parallel to leaf veins. Lesions start on lower leaves, progress upward. Entire plant may turn brown in severe cases.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.treatment_organic:
- Trichoderma harzianum seed treatment @ 4g/kg
- Neem cake @ 100kg/acre soil application
- Crop rotation with non-grass crops
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.treatment_chemical:
**Propiconazole 25 EC @ 1ml/L** — most effective, apply at 10-leaf stage

**Azoxystrobin + Propiconazole (Amistar Top) @ 1ml/L** — premium combination

**Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5g/L** — protective spray, 200L/acre

⚠️ **Critical:** Spray at FIRST appearance on lower leaves. If 50%+ canopy infected — economic spray benefit is limited.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.dosage_summary: Propiconazole 25 EC: 1ml/L · 200L/acre · 10-leaf stage + repeat at tasseling
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.days_to_recovery: Disease progression stops in 10-14 days with spray. Upper leaves remain healthy. Existing lesions do not heal.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.prevention:
- Plant resistant hybrids: DK 9144, Bioseed 9681
- 2-year rotation — avoid maize after maize
- Plough under residue immediately after harvest
- Maintain 60cm row spacing for airflow
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.source: ICAR-IIMR Hyderabad · Northern Leaf Blight Management Advisory

Corn_(maize)___healthy.symptoms: Healthy dark green leaf, no lesions or rust.
Corn_(maize)___healthy.prevention: Monitor weekly. Watch for early rust pustules on lower leaves.

Grape___Black_rot.cause: Fungus: Guignardia bidwellii. Spreads by rain splash. Survives in mummified berries and infected canes. Requires 9+ hours of wetness for infection.
Grape___Black_rot.spread_rate: Can destroy 80-100% of fruit within 3 weeks in wet seasons. One of the most destructive grape diseases in humid climates.
Grape___Black_rot.symptoms: Circular reddish-brown spots on leaves with dark border. Small black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) in lesion centre. Berries turn brown, then shrivel to black 'mummies' that remain attached to cluster.
Grape___Black_rot.treatment_organic:
- Remove all mummified berries before budbreak in February
- Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3g/L from budbreak, every 10 days
- Bordeaux mixture 1% as protective spray
Grape___Black_rot.treatment_chemical:
**Myclobutanil 10 WP @ 1g/L** — most effective systemic, apply from budbreak through berry set

**Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5g/L** — protective spray, 200L/acre, every 7-10 days

**Tebuconazole 25.9 EC @ 1ml/L** — curative if infection established

⚠️ Apply within 48-72 hours after each rainfall event during critical period (pre-bloom to berry set)
⚠️ **Do NOT spray** within 14 days of harvest
Grape___Black_rot.dosage_summary: Myclobutanil 10 WP: 1g/L · 200L/acre · every 7-10 days from budbreak to berry set
Grape___Black_rot.cost_estimate: ₹600–900 per acre for full season program (10-12 sprays)
Grape___Black_rot.days_to_recovery: New berries protected within 5-7 days of spray. Infected berries cannot be saved — remove them.
Grape___Black_rot.prevention:
- Remove all mummies and infected canes during winter pruning
- Train vines for good air circulation
- Apply dormant copper spray before budbreak
- Avoid overhead irrigation

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).cause: Complex of wood-rotting fungi: Phaeoacremonium minimum, Phaeomoniella chlamydospora. Enters through pruning wounds. Systemic — cannot be cured once inside wood.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).spread_rate: Progressive disease — symptoms worsen each year. Affected vines may collapse suddenly ('apoplexy') in summer heat. 10-15% vine loss per year in severely affected vineyards.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).symptoms: Leaves show interveinal yellowing/reddening (tiger-stripe pattern). Berries develop small dark spots, become hard and unmarketable (black measles). Wood shows dark streaking when cut. Sudden vine wilting in hot weather.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).treatment_organic:
**No cure.** Management only:
- Remove severely affected vines immediately
- Protect all pruning wounds with wound sealant or Bordeaux paste
- Prune during dry weather only
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).treatment_chemical:
**No systemic chemical cure available.**

**Wound protection:** Trichoderma asperellum paste on all cut surfaces immediately after pruning

**Preventive:** Thiophanate-methyl 70 WP @ 1.5g/L sprayed on pruning wounds

**Fosetyl-Al 80 WP @ 3g/L** — foliar spray may slow progression but not cure
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).dosage_summary: Thiophanate-methyl: 1.5g/L applied directly to pruning wounds
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).cost_estimate: Wound treatment: ₹200-400 per acre. Vine replacement: ₹15,000-25,000 per acre
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).days_to_recovery: No recovery — affected vines gradually decline. Remove and replant.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).prevention:
- NEVER prune in rain or wet conditions
- Apply wound sealant on every cut immediately
- Use clean, disinfected pruning tools (10% bleach solution)
- Remove and burn infected vines — do not compost
- Plant certified disease-free nursery material
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).source: ICAR Viticulture Research Station Pune · NRCG Pune

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.cause: Fungus: Pseudocercospora vitis (formerly Isariopsis). Survives in infected leaves. Spreads by wind and rain splash. Favoured by warm humid conditions.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.spread_rate: Defoliation can be severe — 40-60% leaf loss in 2-3 weeks in humid seasons, reducing next year's fruit quality.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.symptoms: Irregular dark brown to black spots on upper leaf surface. Lower surface shows olive-brown sporulation. Affected leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely. Premature defoliation weakens vine.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.treatment_organic:
- Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3g/L spray, 200L/acre
- Repeat every 10-14 days from June onwards
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.treatment_chemical:
**Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5g/L** — standard effective spray

**Carbendazim 50 WP @ 1g/L** — systemic option

**Chlorothalonil 75 WP @ 2g/L** — broad-spectrum, good results

⚠️ Begin spraying at first sign of spots, not after defoliation starts
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.days_to_recovery: Leaf drop stops in 14-21 days with spray. New growth remains healthy.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.prevention:
- Remove and destroy fallen leaves
- Ensure good air movement through canopy via proper pruning
- Avoid overhead irrigation

Grape___healthy.symptoms: Healthy green leaf, no spots or lesions.
Grape___healthy.prevention: Continue monitoring weekly. Protect pruning wounds during winter pruning.

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).cause: Bacterial: Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus. Spread ONLY by Asian Citrus Psyllid insect (Diaphorina citri). No soil or contact transmission.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).spread_rate: There is NO CURE. Infected trees decline over 5-10 years and must be destroyed. Disease spreads to neighbouring trees through psyllid insects. Can devastate entire orchards.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).symptoms: Asymmetric yellowing (blotchy mottle) of leaves — yellow patches don't follow leaf veins. Small, lopsided green fruits that never colour properly. Bitter, unpalatable juice. Premature fruit drop. Progressive decline of entire tree.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).treatment_organic:
**NO CURE EXISTS.** Management only:
- Control the psyllid insect vector immediately
- Neem oil 5ml/L spray to reduce psyllid population
- Remove and burn infected trees without delay
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).treatment_chemical:
**For psyllid control (vector management):**

Imidacloprid 17.8 SL @ **0.5ml/L** — soil drench or foliar spray for psyllid

Thiamethoxam 25 WG @ **0.3g/L** — systemic, kills feeding psyllids

**There is NO antibiotic or fungicide that cures HLB once tree is infected.**

⚠️ **Mandatory:** Remove and BURN all infected trees within 48 hours of confirmation — do not delay
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).dosage_summary: Imidacloprid 17.8 SL: 0.5ml/L for psyllid control · soil drench or foliar
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).cost_estimate: Psyllid management: ₹500-800/acre/year. Tree removal and replanting: ₹40,000-60,000/acre
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).days_to_recovery: NO RECOVERY — disease is incurable. Remove infected trees to protect remaining orchard.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).prevention:
- Buy certified disease-free nursery plants ONLY
- Inspect all new plants before bringing to farm
- Monitor for citrus psyllid every 2 weeks
- Never move plant material from infected area
- Control psyllid with quarterly Imidacloprid spray
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).source: ICAR-CCRI Nagpur · National Citrus Disease Management Advisory · Govt of Maharashtra

Peach___Bacterial_spot.cause: Bacteria: Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni. Spreads through rain splash and wind-driven rain. Enters through stomata and wounds.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.spread_rate: Can affect 60-80% of fruit in high-rainfall years. Marketability severely reduced — spotted fruit fetches 40-60% lower price.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small water-soaked spots on leaves that turn angular purple-brown with yellow halo. Leaves develop 'shothole' appearance. Fruit shows sunken, dark pits and cracks. Young twigs develop cankers.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.treatment_organic:
- Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3g/L spray from petal fall
- Repeat every 7-10 days during wet weather
- Bordeaux mixture 0.5% as preventive
Peach___Bacterial_spot.treatment_chemical:
**Copper hydroxide (Kocide) 53.8 DF @ 2g/L** — standard treatment, effective

**Streptomycin sulfate 90 SP @ 0.5g/L** — antibiotic spray, effective on bacteria

**Kasugamycin 3 SL @ 2ml/L** — systemic antibiotic, apply at petal fall and every 10 days

⚠️ Do NOT use copper during bloom — fruit set damage
⚠️ **Do NOT spray** within 30 days of harvest (Streptomycin)
Peach___Bacterial_spot.dosage_summary: Kasugamycin 3 SL: 2ml/L · 200L/acre · every 10 days during wet season
Peach___Bacterial_spot.days_to_recovery: Bacterial spread stops in 7-10 days with copper sprays. Existing lesions remain — protect new growth.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.prevention:
- Plant resistant varieties: Reliance, Harrow Beauty
- Prune out infected wood during dormancy
- Avoid overhead irrigation
- Use wind breaks to reduce rain splash

Peach___healthy.symptoms: Healthy leaf with no spots or lesions.

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.cause: Bacteria: Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria. Spreads through infected seed, rain splash, and farm tools. Survives in crop debris.
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.spread_rate: Can destroy 70-80% of marketable fruit in 2-3 weeks. Entire crop loss possible in severe outbreak with heavy rains.
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small water-soaked spots on leaves with yellow halo, turn brown and dry. Leaves develop shothole. Fruit shows raised, dark-bordered, scabby lesions — unmarketable. Stem cankers cause wilting.
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.treatment_organic:
- Use disease-free certified seed
- Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3g/L spray from transplanting
- Remove infected plants from field immediately
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.treatment_chemical:
**Kasugamycin 3 SL @ 2ml/L** — antibiotic, apply at first symptom

**Copper hydroxide 53.8 DF @ 2g/L** — protective, spray 200L/acre every 7 days

**Streptocycline (Streptomycin + Tetracycline) @ 0.5g/L** — effective bacterial control

⚠️ REMOVE all infected plants to prevent spread
⚠️ Disinfect stakes and farm tools with 1% bleach
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.dosage_summary: Kasugamycin 3 SL: 2ml/L · 200L/acre · every 7 days at first sign
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.cost_estimate: ₹350-550 per acre per spray · 4-6 sprays needed: ₹1,400-3,300 total
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.days_to_recovery: New leaves clean in 10-14 days. Infected fruits cannot be saved.
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.prevention:
- Use certified disease-free seed
- Treat seed with Streptocycline 0.1g/L + Copper oxychloride 3g/L for 30 minutes before sowing
- Avoid overhead irrigation
- Crop rotation — do not grow Solanaceae (pepper, tomato, brinjal) in same field consecutively
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.source: ICAR-IIVR Varanasi · Pepper Disease Management Guide

Pepper,_bell___healthy.prevention: Monitor weekly. Check undersides of leaves for whitefly.

Potato___Early_blight.cause: Fungus: Alternaria solani. Survives in soil and infected debris. Spreads by wind and rain splash. Favours warm days (24-29°C) with cool nights.
Potato___Early_blight.spread_rate: Spreads from lower to upper leaves over 2-3 weeks. Can cause 20-30% yield loss if untreated. More damaging on stressed plants (N deficiency, drought).
Potato___Early_blight.symptoms: Dark brown circular spots (5-15mm) with concentric rings (target board pattern) on older lower leaves. Yellow halo around spots. Premature defoliation from bottom up reduces tuber size.
Potato___Early_blight.treatment_organic:
- Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3g/L spray, 200L/acre
- Start spraying 30-35 days after planting, repeat every 7-10 days
- Remove and destroy infected lower leaves
Potato___Early_blight.treatment_chemical:
**Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5g/L** — most economical, very effective protectant, 200L/acre

**Chlorothalonil 75 WP @ 2g/L** — excellent for wet conditions

**Iprovalicarb + Propineb (Melody Duo) @ 2g/L** — systemic, use when disease established

⚠️ Begin spraying BEFORE disease appears (30 DAS) for best protection
⚠️ **Do NOT spray** within 7 days of harvest
Potato___Early_blight.dosage_summary: Mancozeb 75 WP: 2.5g/L · 200L/acre · every 7-10 days from 30 DAS
Potato___Early_blight.cost_estimate: ₹200-350 per acre per spray · 6-8 sprays: ₹1,200-2,800 per season
Potato___Early_blight.days_to_recovery: New leaves remain healthy in 10-14 days. Affected leaves gradually die — normal plant behaviour. Protect upper canopy.
Potato___Early_blight.prevention:
- Plant certified disease-free seed tubers
- Ensure adequate N fertilization (N-deficient plants most susceptible)
- Avoid water stress during crop growth
- 3-year rotation — avoid potato, tomato, brinjal consecutively
Potato___Early_blight.source: ICAR-CPRI Shimla · Potato Disease Management Manual

Potato___Late_blight.cause: Oomycete (water mould): Phytophthora infestans. The same pathogen that caused the Irish famine of 1845. Spreads explosively through wind-carried spores. Only needs 10-12 hours of wetness to infect.
Potato___Late_blight.spread_rate: **Most dangerous crop disease.** Can destroy entire 1-acre field within 5-7 days in cool (10-20°C) wet weather. One infected plant can infect all neighbours overnight. ICAR reports 70-100% crop loss in epidemic years.
Potato___Late_blight.symptoms: Water-soaked dark green-black lesions appear on leaves overnight — as if boiled. White fluffy sporulation on leaf undersides in humid weather. Stems turn black and collapse. Tubers show brown rot that spreads to storage. Distinctive musty smell.
Potato___Late_blight.treatment_organic:
**Organic control is INSUFFICIENT for late blight — use chemical immediately.**

Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3g/L as preventive spray only

**ACT IMMEDIATELY** — delay of even 2 days allows entire field infection
Potato___Late_blight.treatment_chemical:
**EMERGENCY spray — apply within 24 hours of first symptom:**

**Cymoxanil + Mancozeb (Curzate M8) @ 3g/L** — best combination, curative + protective

**Metalaxyl + Mancozeb (Ridomil Gold) @ 2.5g/L** — systemic, penetrates plant

**Dimethomorph + Mancozeb @ 3g/L** — excellent for established infection

Spray 200L/acre · Repeat EVERY 5-7 DAYS during epidemic conditions

⚠️ **CRITICAL:** Remove infected haulm (tops) 2 weeks before harvest to prevent tuber infection
⚠️ **Do NOT spray** within 7 days of harvest
⚠️ **ROTATE chemicals** — Phytophthora develops resistance quickly
Potato___Late_blight.dosage_summary: Cymoxanil+Mancozeb: 3g/L · 200L/acre · EVERY 5-7 days when disease active
Potato___Late_blight.cost_estimate: ₹450-700 per acre per spray · Emergency program (6-8 sprays): ₹2,700-5,600
Potato___Late_blight.days_to_recovery: Spread stops in 3-5 days with correct chemical. Act immediately — every hour of delay allows wider infection.
Potato___Late_blight.prevention:
- Plant ONLY certified blight-free seed tubers (crucial)
- Plant resistant varieties: Kufri Jyoti, Kufri Bahar, Kufri Lalima
- Begin PREVENTIVE Mancozeb spray 30 DAS — do not wait for symptoms
- Ensure good field drainage — standing water = blight risk
- Destroy culls and volunteers completely
Potato___Late_blight.source: ICAR-CPRI Shimla · Late Blight Emergency Management Protocol · Punjab Agriculture University

Potato___healthy.dosage_summary: No spray needed. Begin preventive Mancozeb spray at 30 DAS as standard practice.
Potato___healthy.prevention: Begin preventive Mancozeb 75 WP (2.5g/L) spray at 30 DAS — do not wait for symptoms. Check weather — spray immediately before forecast rain.

Soybean___healthy.symptoms: Healthy trifoliate leaves, no disease signs.
Soybean___healthy.prevention: Monitor for girdle beetle and yellow mosaic virus weekly. Check stem at 30-35 DAS for girdling.

Squash___Powdery_mildew.cause: Fungi: Podosphaera xanthii / Erysiphe cichoracearum. Spreads by windborne spores. Thrives in warm (20-28°C) dry conditions with high humidity.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.spread_rate: Can cover entire plant surface in 10-14 days. Reduces fruit quality and causes premature plant death. 20-40% yield loss typical.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.symptoms: White powdery patches on upper and lower leaf surfaces. Leaves turn yellow and dry out. Stem and fruit also affected in severe cases.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.treatment_organic:
- Sulfur 80 WP @ 3g/L spray, 200L/acre, every 7 days
- Neem oil 5ml/L + soap 2ml/L spray
- Potassium bicarbonate 5g/L — disrupts fungal cell wall
Squash___Powdery_mildew.treatment_chemical:
**Hexaconazole 5 EC @ 1ml/L** — most effective triazole

**Myclobutanil 10 WP @ 1g/L** — systemic, excellent results

**Triadimefon 25 WP @ 1g/L** — curative for established mildew

⚠️ Do NOT spray sulfur in temperatures above 35°C
⚠️ **Do NOT spray** within 3 days of harvest
Squash___Powdery_mildew.days_to_recovery: White coating fades in 7-10 days. New growth remains healthy.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.prevention:
- Plant resistant varieties when available
- Ensure good spacing and air circulation
- Avoid overhead irrigation in evening hours

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.cause: Fungus: Diplocarpon earlianum. Spreads by rain splash. Infected leaves are primary source. Favours cool wet weather.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.spread_rate: Can defoliate 40-60% of planting in 2-3 weeks. Weakens plants, reduces fruit size and quality.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.symptoms: Small irregular purple to reddish-purple spots on upper leaf. Spots enlarge and centres turn tan/grey with purple borders. Leaves appear scorched. Severe cases cause complete leaf desiccation.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.treatment_organic:
- Remove and destroy infected leaves
- Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3g/L spray
- Ensure adequate air circulation
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.treatment_chemical:
**Myclobutanil 10 WP @ 1g/L** — systemic, effective

**Captan 50 WP @ 2g/L** — protective, spray 200L/acre

**Azoxystrobin 23 SC @ 1ml/L** — excellent for strawberry

⚠️ **Do NOT spray** within 0 days of harvest (Azoxystrobin is safe at harvest)
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.days_to_recovery: Spots stop spreading in 10-14 days. New leaves remain healthy.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.prevention:
- Remove all old leaves and debris before planting new crop
- Avoid overhead irrigation — use drip
- Plant certified disease-free runners only
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.do_not_spray_before_harvest: Check label — most systemic fungicides safe 1-3 days before harvest

Strawberry___healthy.symptoms: Healthy trifoliate leaves, deep green, no spots.
Strawberry___healthy.prevention: Monitor weekly. Check for spider mites on leaf undersides in dry weather.

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.cause: Bacteria: Xanthomonas vesicatoria. Spreads through infected seed, rain splash, pruning tools. Enters through stomata and wounds.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.spread_rate: Can spread to 80% of plants within 10-14 days during rainy season. Fruit spots make entire lot unmarketable. Losses of 30-60% in severe outbreaks.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small water-soaked spots on leaves, turn brown with yellow halo. Shothole appearance. Fruit shows raised, dark-bordered, scabby lesions. Cannot be sold in market.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.treatment_organic:
- Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3g/L spray, every 7 days from transplanting
- Remove and burn infected plants
- Treat seed before sowing
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.treatment_chemical:
**Kasugamycin 3 SL @ 2ml/L** — antibiotic, very effective

**Copper hydroxide 53.8 DF @ 2g/L** + Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2g/L mix — copper + contact fungicide

**Streptocycline 0.5g/L** + Copper oxychloride 3g/L mix — standard treatment

⚠️ Spray at 5-7 day intervals during wet weather
⚠️ Disinfect stakes, cages, and pruning scissors with 1% bleach
⚠️ **Do NOT spray** within 7 days of harvest
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.dosage_summary: Kasugamycin 3 SL: 2ml/L + Copper oxychloride 3g/L · 200L/acre · every 7 days
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.cost_estimate: ₹350-550 per acre per spray · Season program: ₹2,800-4,400
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.days_to_recovery: Spread stops in 7-10 days. New leaves clean in 2 weeks.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.prevention:
- Use certified disease-free seed from reputed company
- Seed treatment: Streptocycline 0.1g/L + Copper oxychloride 3g/L soak for 30 minutes
- Avoid working in field when plants are wet
- Avoid overhead irrigation — use drip

Tomato___Early_blight.cause: Fungus: Alternaria solani. Survives in soil and infected debris. Spreads by wind, rain splash, and farm tools.
Tomato___Early_blight.spread_rate: Defoliates from bottom up over 2-3 weeks. 15-25% yield loss typical. More severe in hot (24-29°C) alternating dry-wet conditions.
Tomato___Early_blight.symptoms: Dark brown circular spots with concentric rings (target board) on older lower leaves. Yellow halo around spots. Stems develop dark sunken lesions. Fruit gets leathery dark lesions at stem end.
Tomato___Early_blight.treatment_organic:
- Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3g/L spray
- Begin 30-35 days after transplanting
- Trichoderma viride soil application @ 1kg per acre
Tomato___Early_blight.treatment_chemical:
**Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5g/L** — most economical and effective, 200L/acre

**Chlorothalonil 75 WP @ 2g/L** — excellent in wet seasons

**Azoxystrobin 23 SC @ 1ml/L** — systemic, good for fruit protection

⚠️ Begin spraying BEFORE disease appears — at transplanting + 30 DAS
⚠️ **Do NOT spray** within 3 days of harvest
Tomato___Early_blight.dosage_summary: Mancozeb 75 WP: 2.5g/L · 200L/acre · every 7-10 days from 30 DAS
Tomato___Early_blight.cost_estimate: ₹200-350 per acre per spray · Full season: ₹1,600-2,800
Tomato___Early_blight.days_to_recovery: New leaves healthy in 10-14 days. Defoliation slows in 7-10 days.
Tomato___Early_blight.prevention:
- Ensure adequate N fertilization (deficient plants most susceptible)
- Remove infected lower leaves every 2 weeks
- Avoid wetting foliage during irrigation
- 2-year rotation away from Solanaceae crops

Tomato___Late_blight.cause: Oomycete: Phytophthora infestans. Same pathogen as potato late blight. Spreads explosively in cool (10-20°C) wet weather.
Tomato___Late_blight.spread_rate: **Fastest spreading crop disease.** Can destroy entire 1-acre field in 5-7 days. In 2023, Maharashtra reported 60-100% tomato crop loss in Nashik due to late blight. One infected plant infects neighbours overnight.
Tomato___Late_blight.symptoms: Water-soaked dark green to black patches on leaves and stems appearing suddenly overnight. White fluffy mould on undersides of leaves in humid conditions. Fruit shows hard, brown-green water-soaked lesions. Entire plant collapses.
Tomato___Late_blight.treatment_organic:
**Organic control is inadequate for late blight — use chemical immediately.**

Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3g/L as preventive spray only.
Tomato___Late_blight.treatment_chemical:
**EMERGENCY — SPRAY WITHIN 24 HOURS:**

**Cymoxanil + Mancozeb (Curzate M8) @ 3g/L** — best combination, 200L/acre

**Metalaxyl + Mancozeb (Ridomil Gold MZ) @ 2.5g/L** — systemic, penetrates plant tissue

**Dimethomorph + Mancozeb @ 3g/L** — excellent resistance management

Repeat EVERY 5-7 DAYS in epidemic conditions

⚠️ **ROTATE chemicals every spray** — resistance develops rapidly
⚠️ Do NOT spray Metalaxyl more than 3 times consecutively
⚠️ **Do NOT spray** within 7 days of harvest
Tomato___Late_blight.cost_estimate: ₹450-700 per acre per spray · Emergency 6-spray program: ₹2,700-4,200
Tomato___Late_blight.days_to_recovery: Spread stops in 3-5 days with correct systemic fungicide. Act immediately.
Tomato___Late_blight.prevention:
- Plant tolerant varieties: Arka Rakshak, Pusa Hybrid-4
- Begin PREVENTIVE Mancozeb spray 30 days after transplanting
- Avoid overhead irrigation
- Ensure good field drainage
- Monitor weather — spray 24 hours before forecast rain
Tomato___Late_blight.source: ICAR-IIVR Varanasi · Maharashtra Late Blight Emergency Protocol 2023

Tomato___Leaf_Miner.cause: Insect: Tuta absoluta (South American leaf miner). Also Liriomyza spp. Larvae mine inside leaves. Very difficult to control once established.
Tomato___Leaf_Miner.spread_rate: Spreads to 50-80% of plants within 2-3 weeks. New generation every 25-30 days. Can cause 80-100% crop loss in severe infestation.
Tomato___Leaf_Miner.symptoms: Whitish serpentine (winding) trails visible inside leaves — larva tunnelling between leaf layers. Affected leaves wither. Small white flies visible on undersides. Fruit also attacked (Tuta absoluta).
Tomato___Leaf_Miner.treatment_organic:
- Yellow sticky traps 10 per acre from transplanting
- Spinosad 45 SC @ 0.3ml/L spray on undersides of leaves
- Neem oil 5ml/L spray weekly
Tomato___Leaf_Miner.treatment_chemical:
**Cyromazine 75 WP @ 0.75g/L** — systemic, translaminates into leaf — kills mining larvae

**Abamectin 1.8 EC @ 0.5ml/L** — contact+systemic, very effective

**Spinosad 45 SC @ 0.3ml/L** — biological-based, effective and safe

Spray 200L/acre, focus on leaf undersides

⚠️ Rotate all 3 chemicals — resistance develops very fast in Tuta absoluta
⚠️ **Do NOT spray** within 3 days of harvest
Tomato___Leaf_Miner.dosage_summary: Cyromazine 75 WP: 0.75g/L · 200L/acre · spray leaf undersides · every 7 days
Tomato___Leaf_Miner.days_to_recovery: New mining stops in 5-7 days. Existing mines remain visible but larvae die.
Tomato___Leaf_Miner.prevention:
- Yellow sticky traps from transplanting onwards
- Net house for nursery — prevents adult entry
- Avoid excessive nitrogen — promotes susceptible soft growth
- Remove infested leaves and destroy
Tomato___Leaf_Miner.source: ICAR-IIVR Varanasi · Tuta absoluta Management Guidelines

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.cause: Fungus: Passalora fulva (Cladosporium fulvum). Spreads only through air — high humidity (>85%) needed for sporulation. Common in greenhouse/poly house tomato.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.spread_rate: Spreads rapidly in poly house conditions — 60-80% plant infection in 14-21 days if humidity not controlled.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.symptoms: Yellow patches on upper leaf surface. Olive-green to brown velvety mold growth on lower leaf corresponding to yellow patches above. Infected leaves wither and die. Plant defoliation from bottom.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.treatment_organic:
- Improve ventilation immediately — reduce humidity below 80%
- Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3g/L spray on undersides
- Trichoderma viride @ 4g/L spray
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.treatment_chemical:
**Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5g/L** — effective contact fungicide, 200L/acre

**Chlorothalonil 75 WP @ 2g/L** — excellent results

**Hexaconazole 5 EC @ 1ml/L** — systemic for poly house

⚠️ Improve ventilation FIRST — without humidity control, sprays give only temporary relief
⚠️ **Do NOT spray** within 3 days of harvest
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.dosage_summary: Chlorothalonil 75 WP: 2g/L · 200L/acre · every 7 days + improve ventilation
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.days_to_recovery: New infection stops in 7-10 days with spray + humidity control.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.prevention:
- Maintain relative humidity below 80% in poly house
- Install exhaust fans and ventilation windows
- Drip irrigation only — avoid wetting foliage
- Plant resistant varieties for poly house

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.cause: Fungus: Septoria lycopersici. Survives on infected debris. Spreads by rain splash. Favours warm (20-25°C) wet weather.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.spread_rate: Defoliates from bottom up over 3-4 weeks. Severe defoliation reduces fruit size and exposes fruit to sunscald. 15-25% yield loss.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.symptoms: Many small circular spots (3-6mm) on lower leaves — water-soaked centres that turn tan/grey with dark brown borders. Tiny black dots (pycnidia) visible in centre of spots with magnifying glass. Leaves turn yellow and drop.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.treatment_organic:
- Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3g/L spray from transplanting
- Remove infected lower leaves every 2 weeks
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.treatment_chemical:
**Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5g/L** — standard effective treatment, 200L/acre

**Chlorothalonil 75 WP @ 2g/L** — excellent for wet conditions

**Azoxystrobin 23 SC @ 1ml/L** — systemic, spray at first sign

⚠️ Spray at 7-day intervals during wet season
⚠️ **Do NOT spray** within 3 days of harvest
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.days_to_recovery: New leaves healthy in 10-14 days. Defoliation rate slows within 7 days of spray.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.prevention:
- Mulch around plant base to prevent soil splash
- Remove infected leaves in lower canopy
- Avoid overhead irrigation
- 2-year rotation away from Solanaceae

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.cause: Mite: Tetranychus urticae. Not a fungus or bacteria — a tiny arachnid pest. Thrives in hot dry conditions. Populations explode rapidly. Do NOT use insecticides — they kill natural enemies and cause mite outbreaks.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.spread_rate: Population doubles every 5-7 days in hot dry weather. Can cover entire plant in fine webbing in 10-14 days. 20-40% yield loss in severe infestation.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.symptoms: Tiny yellowish-green stippling on upper leaf surface. Spider-like webbing on leaf undersides and growing tips. Leaves turn bronze, then brown, and drop. Tiny moving dots visible under magnification on leaf undersides.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.treatment_organic:
- Strong water spray to dislodge mites from undersides daily
- Neem oil 5ml/L + soap 2ml/L spray on leaf undersides every 5 days
- Release predatory mites Phytoseiulus persimilis @ 10-15/plant
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.treatment_chemical:
**Abamectin 1.8 EC @ 0.5ml/L** — most effective miticide, spray leaf undersides

**Fenazaquin 10 EC @ 1.5ml/L** — ovicidal + adulticidal, kills eggs too

**Spiromesifen 22.9 SC @ 1ml/L** — excellent resistance management

⚠️ **NEVER use synthetic pyrethroids (Cypermethrin, Lambda-cyhalothrin)** — kills natural enemies and makes mite problem WORSE
⚠️ **DO NOT use same miticide more than 2 consecutive sprays** — resistance develops fast
⚠️ **Do NOT spray** within 3 days of harvest
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.dosage_summary: Abamectin 1.8 EC: 0.5ml/L · spray LEAF UNDERSIDES only · 200L/acre · every 7 days
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.days_to_recovery: Population crashes in 5-7 days with correct miticide. Apply when population is low — high populations take 14-21 days.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.prevention:
- Irrigate adequately — drought-stressed plants most susceptible
- Avoid excessive nitrogen in summer
- Monitor leaf undersides weekly in March-May
- Conserve natural enemies — avoid broad-spectrum insecticides
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.source: ICAR-IIVR Varanasi · IPM for Mites in Tomato

Tomato___Target_Spot.cause: Fungus: Corynespora cassiicola. Spreads by air and rain splash. Common in humid conditions after rains.
Tomato___Target_Spot.spread_rate: Gradual defoliation over 3-4 weeks. 15-20% yield loss typical. More severe when combined with early blight.
Tomato___Target_Spot.symptoms: Circular brown spots (5-10mm) with concentric rings and yellow halo on leaves. Spot centres may have dark dot pattern. Similar to early blight but spots are more circular and larger.
Tomato___Target_Spot.treatment_chemical:
**Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5g/L** + **Carbendazim 50 WP @ 1g/L** mixed together — excellent combination

**Chlorothalonil 75 WP @ 2g/L** — very effective

**Fluxapyroxad + Pyraclostrobin (Merivon) @ 1ml/L** — premium systemic

⚠️ **Do NOT spray** within 3 days of harvest
Tomato___Target_Spot.prevention:
- Remove infected lower leaves
- Avoid wetting foliage during irrigation
- Good canopy management for airflow

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.cause: Virus transmitted by whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). No soil transmission. Cannot be cured once plant is infected. Whitefly carries virus from infected to healthy plants.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.spread_rate: A single infected whitefly can infect 10-15 plants within hours. Entire field infection possible in 10-14 days if whitefly population is high. **No cure — infected plants must be removed.**
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.symptoms: Youngest leaves show upward curling and yellowing of leaf margins. Leaves become thick, leathery, and cup-shaped. Severe stunting of plant — 50-80% height reduction. Flowers drop, very little fruit set. Plants infected before flowering = total crop loss.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.treatment_organic:
**NO CURE for the virus once infected.**

For whitefly vector control:
- Yellow sticky traps 10 per acre from transplanting
- Neem oil 5ml/L spray on leaf undersides every 5 days
- Remove infected plants immediately — do not leave in field
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.treatment_chemical:
**There is NO chemical that cures TYLCV.**

**Whitefly control (vector management — MUST start at transplanting):**

Imidacloprid 17.8 SL @ **0.5ml/L** — soil drench at transplanting + foliar spray

Thiamethoxam 25 WG @ **0.3g/L** — excellent systemic whitefly control

Dinotefuran 20 SG @ **0.3g/L** — spray at 7-10 day intervals

⚠️ **Remove and burn ALL infected plants** — leaving them in field spreads virus
⚠️ Begin whitefly control from DAY 1 of transplanting — do not wait for symptoms
⚠️ **Do NOT spray** Imidacloprid within 21 days of harvest
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.dosage_summary: Imidacloprid 17.8 SL: 0.5ml/L soil drench at transplanting + 0.5ml/L foliar at 15 and 30 DAS
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.cost_estimate: Whitefly management program: ₹500-800 per acre per season. Infected crop loss: ₹20,000-50,000/acre
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.days_to_recovery: NO RECOVERY for infected plants. Remove immediately. Protect remaining plants with whitefly control.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.prevention:
- Plant TYLCV-resistant varieties: Arka Rakshak, Syngenta Abhinav, Nunhems 2523
- Cover nursery with 50-mesh insect-proof net
- Apply Imidacloprid soil drench at transplanting
- Use reflective silver mulch — repels whitefly
- Inspect field daily for first symptoms — act within 24 hours
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.source: ICAR-IIVR Varanasi · TYLCV National Management Guidelines · Maharashtra Tomato Mission

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.cause: Virus: Tomato mosaic virus. Spreads through contact — contaminated hands, tools, clothing. Also through infected seed. Very stable — survives on dried plant material for years.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.spread_rate: Spreads through touch — one infected plant to all plants touched by same hands/tools without disinfection. Can infect entire field in one pruning session.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.symptoms: Mosaic pattern — light and dark green mottling on young leaves. Leaves may become narrow, fern-like ('fernleaf' symptom). Fruits show internal browning and uneven ripening. Severe stunting and reduced fruit quality.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.treatment_organic:
**NO CURE — prevention only.**

- Remove infected plants immediately
- Wash hands with soap for 20 seconds before working in field after touching infected plant
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.treatment_chemical:
**NO chemical cures mosaic virus.**

**Prevention through seed treatment:** Trisodium phosphate (TSP) 10% seed soak for 15 minutes kills surface virus on seed

**Tool disinfection:** 10% bleach OR 70% alcohol on pruning scissors between plants
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.dosage_summary: Seed treatment: 10% TSP soak 15 minutes. Tool disinfection: 10% bleach between plants.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.cost_estimate: Seed treatment cost: ₹50/kg seed. Infected crop loss: ₹15,000-40,000/acre
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.prevention:
- Use virus-indexed certified seed from reputed company
- Treat seed with 10% trisodium phosphate before sowing
- Never smoke near tomato crop — tobacco mosaic virus can infect tomatoes
- Wash hands before entering field
- Disinfect all pruning tools with bleach between plants

Tomato___healthy.symptoms: Healthy dark green leaf, no spots or lesions.
Tomato___healthy.dosage_summary: Begin preventive Mancozeb 75 WP (2.5g/L) spray 30 days after transplanting as standard protection.
Tomato___healthy.prevention:
- Start preventive fungicide spray at 30 DAS
- Monitor for whitefly weekly — control immediately
- Monitor for early blight from bottom leaves upward
- Drip irrigation only — avoid wetting foliage
